How do we plot the graph of [MATH: y=\arctan x?] As usual, we can use a table of known values.

Content:
In order to determine these known values, let's first look at the graph of the tangent function.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4bca9834048b33b34b51fe3258699f95]

Content:
We see the tangent function is a one-to-one function on the interval [MATH: x\in\left( -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\!.] So if we restrict the domain to this interval, we can define the inverse function [MATH: y=\arctan x.]

Content:
Remember that the inverse swaps the domain and range of the original function. So the domain of [MATH: y=\arctan x] is [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty),] while the range is [MATH: y \in\left( -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\!.] In the domain, we create a table of values:

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following points lies on the graph of the function [MATH: y=\arctan x?]

  1. [MATH: \left(\dfrac\pi 3,\sqrt 3\right)]

  2. [MATH: \left(0, \pi\right)]

  3. [MATH: \left(0,0\right)]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following points lies on the graph of the function [MATH: y=\arctan x?]

1. [MATH: \left(\dfrac\pi 3,\sqrt 3\right)]
2. [MATH: \left(0, \pi\right)]
3. [MATH: \left(0,0\right)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In order for a point [MATH: (a,b)] to lie on the graph of the function [MATH: y=\arctan x,] the following conditions must hold:

  • The reflected point [MATH: (b,a)] must lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x.]

  • The [MATH: y]-value of the point must lie in the range of [MATH: y=\arctan x,] which is [MATH: y\in \left( -\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).]

With this in mind, let's check each of the points.

  • First, we consider the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac\pi 3,\sqrt 3\right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(\sqrt 3,\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x.] [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac\pi 3,\sqrt 3\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arctan x.]

  • Next, we consider the point [MATH: \left(0,\pi\right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(\pi,0\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    • The range of [MATH: y=\arctan x] is [MATH: y\in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),] and [MATH: y=\pi] does not lie within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(\pi, 0\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arctan x.]

  • Finally, we consider the point [MATH: \left(0,0\right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(0,0\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    • The range of [MATH: y=\arctan x] is [MATH: y\in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),] and [MATH: y=0] lies within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(0,0\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\arctan x.]
